title: Stereoselective cyano translocation reaction enabled by photoenzymatic catalysis

paper_content.abstract: Functional-group translocation constitutes a powerful strategy in organic synthesis, allowing precise modification of molecular architectures and functional group positions. Nevertheless, methodologies capable of delivering precise stereocontrol during such migrations remain exceedingly scarce. Herein, we present a photoenzymatic strategy for cyano translocation that achieves precise stereocontrol. The use of stereo-complementary enzymes grants access to both enantiomers, while mechanistic studies and molecular dynamics simulations delineate the origin of stereoselectivity. This work expands the paradigm of transformations that can be rendered asymmetric by photoenzymatic catalysis and provides a new strategy to tackle persistent challenges in organic synthesis.
paper_content.introduction:
Functional groups (FGs) govern the properties and functions of organic molecules, making their introduction, removal, or rearrangement fundamental in organic chemistry1,2. Functional-group translocation enables precise modulation of molecular architecture and FG positioning, with profound effects on biological activity and physicochemical properties, thereby thereby expanding the chemical space for drug discovery and materials design3. In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of radical-mediated migratory processes for key functional groups (FGs), such as aryl, alkynyl, acyloxy, hydroxyl, and cyano groups (CN), in which chemoselectivity and regioselectivity are generally well controlled4–11. Nevertheless, stereocontrol in these reactions has typically relied on chiral substrates, and the direct achievement of precise stereochemical control remains an unresolved challenge (Fig. 1a)12.

Biocatalysis has garnered significant attention in synthesis for its mild, environmentally friendly conditions and inherent stereocontrol13–22. Recently, the incorporation of classical reactive intermediates into enzyme active sites has enabled the development of new-to-nature reactions, particularly those involving highly reactive intermediates such as carbenes and radicals 23–28, thereby broadening the synthetic potential of enzymatic catalysis. Flavin-dependent enzymes represent one of the most prevalent classes of enzymes in nature, orchestrating a broad spectrum of biological redox transformations29. These enzymes facilitate processes including substrate dehydrogenation, monooxygenation, cyclization, and intricate radical-mediated reactions, thereby playing central roles in energy metabolism, signal transduction, and the biosynthesis of diverse natural products30. Flavins exhibit exceptional versatility due to their ability to adopt multiple redox states, including oxidized, single-electron reduced, and two-electron reduced forms31–37. Recent developments have harnessed photoexcitation to enhance their redox capabilities, enabling radical-mediated coupling reactions with precise stereochemical control38–47. Flavin-dependent photoenzymatic catalysis typically proceeds through radical addition to alkenes38,39. More recently, the reaction paradigm has been extended to radical additions to nitro compounds41 and oximes48, as well as radical-mediated 1,5-hydrogen atom transfer (1,5-HAT) reactions (Fig. 1b)49. Nevertheless, alternative pathways within this enzymatic class remain largely unexplored.

We aimed to exploit flavin-dependent enzymes to catalyze stereoselective functional group translocation reactions. Alkyl nitriles are highly valuable synthetic intermediates, as they can be readily transformed into carboxylic acids, amines, and numerous other functional molecules50–52. Consequently, the development of enantioenriched alkyl nitriles is of considerable significance in both academia and industry.
paper_content.results:
The excited state of flavin hydroquinone (FMN*) possesses a reduction potential of approximately −2.26 V vs SCE53, which enables the reduction of alkyl iodides (E ≈ −2.19 V vs SCE)54. This redox compatibility prompted us to select 5-iodo-2-methyl-2-phenylpentanenitrile 1a as a model substrate to evaluate the feasibility of the CN translocation reaction. Inspired by chemical precedents, our design involves the generation of a neutral alkyl radical within the enzyme active site, which enables addition to the C≡N bond followed by β-fragmentation of the resulting iminyl radical to effect CN migration7–9. The ensuing radical is subsequently quenched via enzyme-catalyzed stereoselective hydrogen atom transfer (HAT), thereby providing access to chiral alkyl nitriles with high stereocontrol (Fig. 1c).

In this work, we selected CN translocation as a representative transformation. Initially, we screened a panel of flavin-dependent enzymes and found that several displayed measurable catalytic activities (Table 1). Among them, old yellow enzyme 1 from Saccharomyces pastorianus (OYE1) catalyzed the formation of the product in 30% yield with 43:57 (S:R) stereoselectivity, whereas old yellow enzyme 3 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (OYE3) afforded a 27% yield with 45:55 e.r. The optimal result was achieved with Caulobacter segnis arene reductase from Caulobacter segnis (CsER), providing the S-configured product in 69% yield and 98:2 e.r. In contrast, enoate reductase from Gluconobacter oxydans (GluER) afforded the opposite stereoisomer in 57% yield with 1:99 e.r. Control experiments were then performed, as shown in Table 1, entry 5-8. No product was detected in the absence of the enzyme, GDH, or light, indicating that the transformation relies on the excited FMNhq. When the enzymes were replaced with FMN alone, only trace amounts of product were formed without stereoselectivity, highlighting the indispensable role of enzyme scaffold in orchestrating both reactivity and stereocontrol. While our manuscript was under revision, Yang reported a similar cyano migration reaction catalyzed by an NADPH-dependent imine reductase55.

With the optimal reaction conditions in hand, we explored the substrate scope for this photoenzymatic CN translocation reaction. As shown in Fig. 2, substrates bearing either electron-rich (S)-2b-2e or electron-deficient substituents (S)-2f-2g on the phenyl ring were tolerated, delivering products with good reactivity and stereoselectivity. The disubstituted aromatic substrate 1e was also efficiently converted into (S)-2e in 53% yield with 90:10 e.r. In addition to the benzyl-position methyl group, the ethyl-substituted substrate 1h was evaluated, which afforded the corresponding product (S)-2h in 65% yield with 97:3 e.r. Furthermore, substrates bearing larger alkyl groups at benzyl position (R=i-Pr (1i) and Cy (1j)) were not well tolerated. Sterically demanding naphthyl substrate 1k was accommodated in the reaction, affording product (S)-2k in 24% yield with 98:2 e.r. Compounds bearing heterocyclic substituents were well tolerated, affording the pyridine-substituted product (S)-2l in 65% yield with 99:1 e.r. and the thiophene-substituted product (S)-2m in 63% yield with 97:3 e.r. Benzyl-substituted substrates were further examined to expand the substrate scope. The dicyano-substituted benzyl derivative (1n) reacted with moderate yield and decreased stereoselectivity (Table S5). We further employed 1n as a substrate to screen and evolve flavin-dependent enzymes, and identified OYE3-Y196F as the improved mutant, affording (R)-2n in 70% yield and 85:15 e.r. (Table S6). We hypothesize that the reduced stereoselectivity of these substrates may result from accelerated radical quenching facilitated by electron-withdrawing cyano groups. Consistent with this hypothesis, introducing electron-donating groups on the phenyl ring enhanced stereoselectivity ((R)-2o, (R)-2p and (R)-2q), whereas electron-withdrawing groups further diminished it ((R)-2t: 85% yield, 70:30 e.r.), underscoring the critical role of electronic effects in governing stereocontrol. Benzyl ester-substituted substrate 1u also underwent the reaction, providing the desired products (R)-2u in good yields with moderate stereoselectivity. Finally, we examined the reversed-selectivity reactions catalyzed by GluER, identified in the initial screening, and found that its substrate scope was highly limited ((R)-2a: 57% yield, 1:99 e.r.; (R)-2f: 35% yield, 14:86 e.r.). Finally, the scaled-up reaction (0.1 mmol of 1d) was implemented, affording the corresponding product in 50% yield and 99:1 e.r.

To gain insight into the mechanism of this transformation, we carried out a series of control experiments. Radical trapping experiments employing TEMPO significantly suppressed the product yield (Fig. 3a) and enabled the detection of the corresponding TEMPO-substrate adduct (Section 5.2 in SI). This result suggests that the reaction proceeds via a radical pathway. Furthermore, the reaction maintained a yield of 32% even in the presence of TEMPO. This result likely stems from the generation of the alkyl radical intermediate within the confined enzyme pocket, where intramolecular CN trapping is more readily achieved than intermolecular quenching by TEMPO. UV–visible spectroscopy revealed that FMN alone exhibits no absorption in the visible region, whereas the addition of the substrate induces the formation of a distinct Electron Donor-Acceptor (EDA) complex, enhancing the system’s absorption under visible light (Fig. 3b). Experiments were conducted of alkene substrates (1w and 1v) with different carbon-chain lengths. As shown in Fig. 3c, deiodinated products from direct hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) were detected, whereas no cyano migration products were observed (Section 5.5 in SI). To further probe the mechanistic basis of this observation, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed on cluster models composed of FMN and the corresponding deiodinated radical intermediates (Fig. S15–S17). The results reveal that the 1,4-cyano translocation pathway of 1a, proceeding via a five-membered cyclic radical intermediate, is energetically favored, in good agreement with the experimental observations. Isotopic labeling experiments were carried out to probe the reaction quenching pathway. No deuterium incorporation was observed in the product using a deuterated buffer. By contrast, in situ generation of deuterated flavin semiquinone (FMNsq) from deuterated glucose led to 56% deuterium incorporation (Fig. 3d), supporting that quenching occurs via FMNsq.

To elucidate the origin of stereoselectivity in this new-to-nature enzymatic reaction at the molecular level, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were conducted. As the final HAT process determined the stereoselectivity of products, we focused on the stage that the β-fragmentation of the iminyl radical has achieved, with the cofactor under the FMNsq state (Fig. 3e). The RMSD profiles of all binding components and the key distance between the HAT involved atoms, i.e., H5 of FMNsq and C7 of 2a', became converged within 200 ns. However, the dihedral formed by the coplanar C3, C8, and C7 of 2a' and the H5 of FMNsq (∠C3-C8-C7-H5), an indicator of the hydrogen atom incorporation via a re or si face, showed a highly biased distribution (Figs. S4 and S5), which agrees well with the experimentally determined e.r values. The representative binding conformations demonstrated consistent binding features. The cyano group of 2a' anchored to a polar environment built mainly by the H173/H172 and N176/N175 side chains in CsER/GluER in almost all cases. Relative to the pro-(R) binding form, the benzyl group of pro-(S) 2a' formed additional parallel π-π stacking interactions with Y66 (Fig. S8), providing extra binding stability. In binding with GluER, two π-π stacking interactions were observed for both the pro-(R) (with W66 and W342) and pro-(S) (with W66 and F269) 2a'. However, the distances of the pro-(S) 2a' involved π-π stacking are relatively longer than that of the pro-(R) 2a' (Fig. 3e and Fig. S10), indicating a decreased binding strength. For the dicyano-substituted intermediate 2n', a distinct binding feature was discovered in its binding with OYE3 (Y196F), i.e., the H5 atom is almost always coplanar with the radical plane of 2n' (defined by atoms C3, C7, and C8, Fig. S7), leading to a concentrated distribution of dihedral angles around 180° and –180° and a decreased conformational preference (Fig. S6). In comparison with the pro-(S) 2n', the pro-(R) binding form is more favorable by forming a sandwich framework with Y82 and Y375 through π-π stacking interactions, resulting in a dihedral distribution which is in accordance with the stereoselectivity of OYE3 (Y196F) (Figs. S6 and S7). Notably, with the cyano group of 2a'/2n' stably anchored to the polar residues His and/or Asn through hydrogen bond interactions in all binding systems, the prochiral conversion can be primarily attributed to the rotation of the C7‒C8 bond. Together, MD simulations shed light on the mechanism of stereoselective cyano translocation.
paper_content.methods:
Flavin-dependent enzyme catalyzed cyano translocation reaction

960 μL Enzyme solution (0.025–0.03 μmol pure enzyme, 1 mol%, tris buffer, pH = 8.0) contain NADP+ (7 μL, 0.1 μmol, 15 mM stock in buffer, 3 mol%), GDH (100 μL, about 3 U, 30 U/mL stock in buffer), glucose (100 μmol, 33.3 equiv) was added to a 10 mL Schlenk tube containing a magnetic stir bar. 1 (3 μmol, 1.0 equiv) in DMSO (40 μL) was following added into the system. The mixture was then degassed by freeze-pump-thaw for three times under N2 atmosphere. The reaction was stirred for 12 h at room temperature. Then the reaction was extracted by ethyl acetate for three times (1 mL × 3). The enantioselectivity was determined by GC or HPLC.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Functional group migration offers a powerful approach for precise molecular editing and regiocontrol, yet strategies that achieve exact stereochemical control remain rare. Professor Jian Xu and co-workers have introduced a photoenzymatic cyano migration that enables precise stereocontrol. By employing stereocomplementary enzymes, both enantiomers of the product can be accessed—a selectivity rationalized through mechanistic studies and molecular dynamics simulations. This work significantly broadens the scope of asymmetric transformations achievable via photoenzymatic catalysis and presents a compelling strategy to address long-standing challenges in organic synthesis. Overall, this reviewer finds the MS highly exciting and looks forward to future advances from the authors.
1. Regarding the substrate scope, electron-withdrawing substituents lead to diminished yield and enantioselectivity. The manuscript merely suggests accelerated radical quenching as a possible cause, which does not sufficiently account for the significantly low yields. A mass balance analysis is recommended to clarify the fate of the substrates.
2. In the radical trapping experiment, the reaction yield remains at 32% despite the addition of 4 equivalents of TEMPO. Any discussions would be helpful.
3. Additional review could be cited, such as Chin. J. Chem. 2024, DOI: 10.1002/cjoc.202400656
4. The Supporting Information lacks detailed procedures for the substrate synthesis and enzymatic reactions.
5. For racemic product 2o in Table S65 (line 990), the high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) deviation exceeds 0.001 Da. Re-measurement is suggested.
6. Several NMR spectra in the SI are misinterpreted. For example, in the spectrum of racemic 2g (S92), the aromatic region is incorrectly integrated to 2.77H, and an extra hydrogen is accounted for in the aliphatic region. Similarly, in the spectrum of 2h (S93), a water peak appears to have been misassigned as a product signal. A thorough re-examination of all spectral assignments is suggested.
7. Minor errors were noted in the SI: inconsistent font type at S3 line 44, "standard" misspelled in the table on S17, and inconsistent abbreviation of "eq" in the first reaction scheme on S21. A full proofreading is recommended to ensure consistency and accuracy throughout.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript by Wang and Xu describes a photoenzymatic 1,5-cyano transfer reaction catalyzed by flavin-dependent ene-reductases. While these types of cyano transfer reactions are well known in the photoredox literature, they have not been realized within a photoenzyme. The ERED platform is well established for photoenzymatic reactivity and can control the delivery of a hydrogen atom to prochiral benzylic radicals with excellent enantioselectivity, making it a sensible catalyst for the reported reaction. The yields and enantioselectivities are good with a range of substates. Mechanistic studies confirm that radical initiation occurs via excitation of charge transfer complex. Overall, I would describe this work as novel but not particularly surprising as it relies on many well-established features from the ERED photoenzymatic literature.

- Is there a kinetic resolution of the racemic starting material?
- Does the method tolerate pyridine as an arene?
- Are larger alkyl groups (beyond methyl) tolerated by the enzyme?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This work introduces a photoenzymatic strategy for stereocontrolled translocation reactions, with cyano translocation taken as a model system. It combines experimental data with computational analysis aimed at rationalizing the stereoselectivity. At this stage, however, the computational component does not appear sufficiently strong, as it is not entirely clear whether the sampling depth and methodological rigor of the analysis are adequate to support firm mechanistic conclusions. Nevertheless, if the results can be maintained and strengthened after addressing the following comments, the study may reach the level required for publication. I would like to see the revised version of the manuscript.
1) The simulations need to be extended and at least a second replica needs to be performed for each systems.
2) Rather than showing distances from a single representative configuration (such as those between the substrate and the polar atoms of the active site, or between the benzyl ring and hydrophobic active-site residues), the authors should present the distribution of each distance over the course of the MD simulation, separated for the pro-S and pro-R basins.
3) One of the main conclusions drawn from the simulations is the following:
“Notably, the benzyl group formed additional parallel (with W100) and T-shaped (with F269) π-π stacking interactions in the pro-(S) binding form in CsER and the pro-(R) binding form in GluER, respectively, providing extra binding stability. In contrast, the pro-(R) binding form in CsER and the pro-(S) binding form in GluER showed much more exposure of the 2a• hydrophobic group to polar water molecules, indicative of an energetically unfavorable binding mode.”
This could be an interesting observation but should be corroborated by specific analyses.
a) Concerning the distances between the benzyl group and hydrophobic residues, the authors should also consider the side chains of residues that could for pi-pi interactions in the “wrong” pro-chiral basin as for example:
-distance between the benzyl group and Y336 or Y66 in CsER (pro-R)
-distance between the benzyl group and W66 and W342 in GluER (pro-S)
b) Concerning the comment on the larger exposure to water molecules of hydrophobic groups, this should be shown with appropriate analyses
4) Concerning the OYE3 enzyme, the authors claim: “the dihedral distribution and structure characteristics in the binding complex of OYE3(Y196F), FMNsq, and 2i• were in accordance with the reduced stereoselectivity for the dicyano-substituted compounds (Fig. S6).”
I might agree with this conclusion, but not for the reasons provided by the authors. In fact, for OYE3-Y196F the negative values do not appear to be pro-S but rather achiral, as they lie too close to –180° to define a clear prochiral preference. Similarly, for the positive values the average dihedral angle may also be not too far from 180°, which again implies an unclear chiral assignment. The authors may therefore wish to reconsider and revise their interpretation.
Minor points:
Which software was used for optimizations at the DFT level?
Why was the e Berendsen barostat used?
Which thermostat was used?
Which software (or in-house script?) was used for the clustering analysis?
Which atoms were chosen for the fit in the RMSD calculations for each of the three components?
The y label in Figure S4, panel b, should be distance, not RMSD.
Some data on the clustering analysis should be reported to better understand the choice of the representative structure.
“Substrate scope of for the photoenzymatic enantioselective CN translocation reaction”. “for” needs to be deleted.
What do the authors mean with “solute” in the sentence “with a weak constraint of 10 kcal∙mol-1∙Å -2 imposed on the solute “?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
Xu et al reported an interesting cyano translocation reaction with high stereoselectivity under the photoenzymatic catalysis with ene reductases. But it seems this reaction only works with three carbons, limiting its synthetic applications. It did not work with four carbon atoms, possibly due the stability of six-membered cyclic radical intermediate. It is not clear whether it works with other numbers of carbon atoms, that may be dependent on the ability of forming the cyclic intermediate and the stability of the intermediate. The computational analysis may address this point.
Table 2, CsER or GluER is noted in the footnote, but it is not noted which one under each product. It should be noted under each product for clarity.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Functional-group translocation constitutes a powerful strategy in organic synthesis, allowing precise modification of molecular architectures and functional group positions. Nevertheless, methodologies capable of delivering precise stereocontrol during such migrations remain exceedingly scarce. Herein, we present a photoenzymatic strategy for cyano translocation that achieves precise stereocontrol. The use of stereo-complementary enzymes grants access to both enantiomers, while mechanistic studies and molecular dynamics simulations delineate the origin of stereoselectivity. This work expands the paradigm of transformations that can be rendered asymmetric by photoenzymatic catalysis and provides a new strategy to tackle persistent challenges in organic synthesis.

---

## Introduction

Functional groups (FGs) govern the properties and functions of organic molecules, making their introduction, removal, or rearrangement fundamental in organic chemistry1,2. Functional-group translocation enables precise modulation of molecular architecture and FG positioning, with profound effects on biological activity and physicochemical properties, thereby thereby expanding the chemical space for drug discovery and materials design3. In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of radical-mediated migratory processes for key functional groups (FGs), such as aryl, alkynyl, acyloxy, hydroxyl, and cyano groups (CN), in which chemoselectivity and regioselectivity are generally well controlled4–11. Nevertheless, stereocontrol in these reactions has typically relied on chiral substrates, and the direct achievement of precise stereochemical control remains an unresolved challenge (Fig. 1a)12.

Biocatalysis has garnered significant attention in synthesis for its mild, environmentally friendly conditions and inherent stereocontrol13–22. Recently, the incorporation of classical reactive intermediates into enzyme active sites has enabled the development of new-to-nature reactions, particularly those involving highly reactive intermediates such as carbenes and radicals 23–28, thereby broadening the synthetic potential of enzymatic catalysis. Flavin-dependent enzymes represent one of the most prevalent classes of enzymes in nature, orchestrating a broad spectrum of biological redox transformations29. These enzymes facilitate processes including substrate dehydrogenation, monooxygenation, cyclization, and intricate radical-mediated reactions, thereby playing central roles in energy metabolism, signal transduction, and the biosynthesis of diverse natural products30. Flavins exhibit exceptional versatility due to their ability to adopt multiple redox states, including oxidized, single-electron reduced, and two-electron reduced forms31–37. Recent developments have harnessed photoexcitation to enhance their redox capabilities, enabling radical-mediated coupling reactions with precise stereochemical control38–47. Flavin-dependent photoenzymatic catalysis typically proceeds through radical addition to alkenes38,39. More recently, the reaction paradigm has been extended to radical additions to nitro compounds41 and oximes48, as well as radical-mediated 1,5-hydrogen atom transfer (1,5-HAT) reactions (Fig. 1b)49. Nevertheless, alternative pathways within this enzymatic class remain largely unexplored.

We aimed to exploit flavin-dependent enzymes to catalyze stereoselective functional group translocation reactions. Alkyl nitriles are highly valuable synthetic intermediates, as they can be readily transformed into carboxylic acids, amines, and numerous other functional molecules50–52. Consequently, the development of enantioenriched alkyl nitriles is of considerable significance in both academia and industry.

## Paper

## Abstract

Functional-group translocation constitutes a powerful strategy in organic synthesis, allowing precise modification of molecular architectures and functional group positions. Nevertheless, methodologies capable of delivering precise stereocontrol during such migrations remain exceedingly scarce. Herein, we present a photoenzymatic strategy for cyano translocation that achieves precise stereocontrol. The use of stereo-complementary enzymes grants access to both enantiomers, while mechanistic studies and molecular dynamics simulations delineate the origin of stereoselectivity. This work expands the paradigm of transformations that can be rendered asymmetric by photoenzymatic catalysis and provides a new strategy to tackle persistent challenges in organic synthesis.

---

## Introduction

Functional groups (FGs) govern the properties and functions of organic molecules, making their introduction, removal, or rearrangement fundamental in organic chemistry1,2. Functional-group translocation enables precise modulation of molecular architecture and FG positioning, with profound effects on biological activity and physicochemical properties, thereby thereby expanding the chemical space for drug discovery and materials design3. In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of radical-mediated migratory processes for key functional groups (FGs), such as aryl, alkynyl, acyloxy, hydroxyl, and cyano groups (CN), in which chemoselectivity and regioselectivity are generally well controlled4–11. Nevertheless, stereocontrol in these reactions has typically relied on chiral substrates, and the direct achievement of precise stereochemical control remains an unresolved challenge (Fig. 1a)12.

Biocatalysis has garnered significant attention in synthesis for its mild, environmentally friendly conditions and inherent stereocontrol13–22. Recently, the incorporation of classical reactive intermediates into enzyme active sites has enabled the development of new-to-nature reactions, particularly those involving highly reactive intermediates such as carbenes and radicals 23–28, thereby broadening the synthetic potential of enzymatic catalysis. Flavin-dependent enzymes represent one of the most prevalent classes of enzymes in nature, orchestrating a broad spectrum of biological redox transformations29. These enzymes facilitate processes including substrate dehydrogenation, monooxygenation, cyclization, and intricate radical-mediated reactions, thereby playing central roles in energy metabolism, signal transduction, and the biosynthesis of diverse natural products30. Flavins exhibit exceptional versatility due to their ability to adopt multiple redox states, including oxidized, single-electron reduced, and two-electron reduced forms31–37. Recent developments have harnessed photoexcitation to enhance their redox capabilities, enabling radical-mediated coupling reactions with precise stereochemical control38–47. Flavin-dependent photoenzymatic catalysis typically proceeds through radical addition to alkenes38,39. More recently, the reaction paradigm has been extended to radical additions to nitro compounds41 and oximes48, as well as radical-mediated 1,5-hydrogen atom transfer (1,5-HAT) reactions (Fig. 1b)49. Nevertheless, alternative pathways within this enzymatic class remain largely unexplored.

We aimed to exploit flavin-dependent enzymes to catalyze stereoselective functional group translocation reactions. Alkyl nitriles are highly valuable synthetic intermediates, as they can be readily transformed into carboxylic acids, amines, and numerous other functional molecules50–52. Consequently, the development of enantioenriched alkyl nitriles is of considerable significance in both academia and industry.

---

## Results

The excited state of flavin hydroquinone (FMN*) possesses a reduction potential of approximately −2.26 V vs SCE53, which enables the reduction of alkyl iodides (E ≈ −2.19 V vs SCE)54. This redox compatibility prompted us to select 5-iodo-2-methyl-2-phenylpentanenitrile 1a as a model substrate to evaluate the feasibility of the CN translocation reaction. Inspired by chemical precedents, our design involves the generation of a neutral alkyl radical within the enzyme active site, which enables addition to the C≡N bond followed by β-fragmentation of the resulting iminyl radical to effect CN migration7–9. The ensuing radical is subsequently quenched via enzyme-catalyzed stereoselective hydrogen atom transfer (HAT), thereby providing access to chiral alkyl nitriles with high stereocontrol (Fig. 1c).

In this work, we selected CN translocation as a representative transformation. Initially, we screened a panel of flavin-dependent enzymes and found that several displayed measurable catalytic activities (Table 1). Among them, old yellow enzyme 1 from Saccharomyces pastorianus (OYE1) catalyzed the formation of the product in 30% yield with 43:57 (S:R) stereoselectivity, whereas old yellow enzyme 3 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (OYE3) afforded a 27% yield with 45:55 e.r. The optimal result was achieved with Caulobacter segnis arene reductase from Caulobacter segnis (CsER), providing the S-configured product in 69% yield and 98:2 e.r. In contrast, enoate reductase from Gluconobacter oxydans (GluER) afforded the opposite stereoisomer in 57% yield with 1:99 e.r. Control experiments were then performed, as shown in Table 1, entry 5-8. No product was detected in the absence of the enzyme, GDH, or light, indicating that the transformation relies on the excited FMNhq. When the enzymes were replaced with FMN alone, only trace amounts of product were formed without stereoselectivity, highlighting the indispensable role of enzyme scaffold in orchestrating both reactivity and stereocontrol. While our manuscript was under revision, Yang reported a similar cyano migration reaction catalyzed by an NADPH-dependent imine reductase55.

With the optimal reaction conditions in hand, we explored the substrate scope for this photoenzymatic CN translocation reaction. As shown in Fig. 2, substrates bearing either electron-rich (S)-2b-2e or electron-deficient substituents (S)-2f-2g on the phenyl ring were tolerated, delivering products with good reactivity and stereoselectivity. The disubstituted aromatic substrate 1e was also efficiently converted into (S)-2e in 53% yield with 90:10 e.r. In addition to the benzyl-position methyl group, the ethyl-substituted substrate 1h was evaluated, which afforded the corresponding product (S)-2h in 65% yield with 97:3 e.r. Furthermore, substrates bearing larger alkyl groups at benzyl position (R=i-Pr (1i) and Cy (1j)) were not well tolerated. Sterically demanding naphthyl substrate 1k was accommodated in the reaction, affording product (S)-2k in 24% yield with 98:2 e.r. Compounds bearing heterocyclic substituents were well tolerated, affording the pyridine-substituted product (S)-2l in 65% yield with 99:1 e.r. and the thiophene-substituted product (S)-2m in 63% yield with 97:3 e.r. Benzyl-substituted substrates were further examined to expand the substrate scope. The dicyano-substituted benzyl derivative (1n) reacted with moderate yield and decreased stereoselectivity (Table S5). We further employed 1n as a substrate to screen and evolve flavin-dependent enzymes, and identified OYE3-Y196F as the improved mutant, affording (R)-2n in 70% yield and 85:15 e.r. (Table S6). We hypothesize that the reduced stereoselectivity of these substrates may result from accelerated radical quenching facilitated by electron-withdrawing cyano groups. Consistent with this hypothesis, introducing electron-donating groups on the phenyl ring enhanced stereoselectivity ((R)-2o, (R)-2p and (R)-2q), whereas electron-withdrawing groups further diminished it ((R)-2t: 85% yield, 70:30 e.r.), underscoring the critical role of electronic effects in governing stereocontrol. Benzyl ester-substituted substrate 1u also underwent the reaction, providing the desired products (R)-2u in good yields with moderate stereoselectivity. Finally, we examined the reversed-selectivity reactions catalyzed by GluER, identified in the initial screening, and found that its substrate scope was highly limited ((R)-2a: 57% yield, 1:99 e.r.; (R)-2f: 35% yield, 14:86 e.r.). Finally, the scaled-up reaction (0.1 mmol of 1d) was implemented, affording the corresponding product in 50% yield and 99:1 e.r.

To gain insight into the mechanism of this transformation, we carried out a series of control experiments. Radical trapping experiments employing TEMPO significantly suppressed the product yield (Fig. 3a) and enabled the detection of the corresponding TEMPO-substrate adduct (Section 5.2 in SI). This result suggests that the reaction proceeds via a radical pathway. Furthermore, the reaction maintained a yield of 32% even in the presence of TEMPO. This result likely stems from the generation of the alkyl radical intermediate within the confined enzyme pocket, where intramolecular CN trapping is more readily achieved than intermolecular quenching by TEMPO. UV–visible spectroscopy revealed that FMN alone exhibits no absorption in the visible region, whereas the addition of the substrate induces the formation of a distinct Electron Donor-Acceptor (EDA) complex, enhancing the system’s absorption under visible light (Fig. 3b). Experiments were conducted of alkene substrates (1w and 1v) with different carbon-chain lengths. As shown in Fig. 3c, deiodinated products from direct hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) were detected, whereas no cyano migration products were observed (Section 5.5 in SI). To further probe the mechanistic basis of this observation, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed on cluster models composed of FMN and the corresponding deiodinated radical intermediates (Fig. S15–S17). The results reveal that the 1,4-cyano translocation pathway of 1a, proceeding via a five-membered cyclic radical intermediate, is energetically favored, in good agreement with the experimental observations. Isotopic labeling experiments were carried out to probe the reaction quenching pathway. No deuterium incorporation was observed in the product using a deuterated buffer. By contrast, in situ generation of deuterated flavin semiquinone (FMNsq) from deuterated glucose led to 56% deuterium incorporation (Fig. 3d), supporting that quenching occurs via FMNsq.

To elucidate the origin of stereoselectivity in this new-to-nature enzymatic reaction at the molecular level, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were conducted. As the final HAT process determined the stereoselectivity of products, we focused on the stage that the β-fragmentation of the iminyl radical has achieved, with the cofactor under the FMNsq state (Fig. 3e). The RMSD profiles of all binding components and the key distance between the HAT involved atoms, i.e., H5 of FMNsq and C7 of 2a', became converged within 200 ns. However, the dihedral formed by the coplanar C3, C8, and C7 of 2a' and the H5 of FMNsq (∠C3-C8-C7-H5), an indicator of the hydrogen atom incorporation via a re or si face, showed a highly biased distribution (Figs. S4 and S5), which agrees well with the experimentally determined e.r values. The representative binding conformations demonstrated consistent binding features. The cyano group of 2a' anchored to a polar environment built mainly by the H173/H172 and N176/N175 side chains in CsER/GluER in almost all cases. Relative to the pro-(R) binding form, the benzyl group of pro-(S) 2a' formed additional parallel π-π stacking interactions with Y66 (Fig. S8), providing extra binding stability. In binding with GluER, two π-π stacking interactions were observed for both the pro-(R) (with W66 and W342) and pro-(S) (with W66 and F269) 2a'. However, the distances of the pro-(S) 2a' involved π-π stacking are relatively longer than that of the pro-(R) 2a' (Fig. 3e and Fig. S10), indicating a decreased binding strength. For the dicyano-substituted intermediate 2n', a distinct binding feature was discovered in its binding with OYE3 (Y196F), i.e., the H5 atom is almost always coplanar with the radical plane of 2n' (defined by atoms C3, C7, and C8, Fig. S7), leading to a concentrated distribution of dihedral angles around 180° and –180° and a decreased conformational preference (Fig. S6). In comparison with the pro-(S) 2n', the pro-(R) binding form is more favorable by forming a sandwich framework with Y82 and Y375 through π-π stacking interactions, resulting in a dihedral distribution which is in accordance with the stereoselectivity of OYE3 (Y196F) (Figs. S6 and S7). Notably, with the cyano group of 2a'/2n' stably anchored to the polar residues His and/or Asn through hydrogen bond interactions in all binding systems, the prochiral conversion can be primarily attributed to the rotation of the C7‒C8 bond. Together, MD simulations shed light on the mechanism of stereoselective cyano translocation.

Reviewer’s general comments:
Xu et al reported an interesting cyano translocation reaction with high stereoselectivity under the
photoenzymatic catalysis with ene reductases. But it seems this reaction only works with three
carbons, limiting its synthetic applications. It did not work with four carbon atoms, possibly due the

and the stability of the intermediate. The computational analysis may address this point.
Our response:
Thank you for your valuable comment.
To examine the feasibility of four-, six-, and seven-membered cyclic radical intermediates in the
reaction, we conducted experiments using substrates 1w, 1v, and 1x. As shown in the figure below,
only products resulting from direct HAT after deiodination were observed, and no products arising
from CN migration were detected. We have added this content to the Supplementary Information
(Page S38, Section 5.5).
To elucidate why the stereoselective cyano translocation reaction favors substrate with 1a (five-
membered cyclic radical intermediates), DFT calculations were performed on the cluster models
composed of FMN and the deiodinated radical intermediates derived from 1w, 1a, and 1v,
sq
corresponding to the potential formation of four-, five-, and six-membered cyclic radical
intermediates. Two plausible reaction pathways were investigated: the formation of cyclic
intermediates and direct quenching through HAT. The results demonstrate that only the intermediate
derived from 1a favors the cyclic intermediate pathway with an energy barrier of 4.21 kcal/mol,
which is 3.31 kcal/mol less than the HAT pathway (Fig. S12). For the intermediate derived from 1w
and 1v, the cyclic intermediate pathway shows obviously higher energy barriers than the
corresponding HAT pathway (Fig. S13 and S14). The DFT results agree well with our experimental
findings and explain the reaction preference for the substrates which are able to form five-membered
cyclic intermediate. This result has been included in the Supplementary Information (Page S50-S52,
Section 5.7). Additionally, we have added the following sentence in the main text: “DFT calculations
further corroborate that the 1,4-CN translocation pathway is energetically preferred.”.
